extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys) evaluating/defending 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining what qualifies as prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 (including 102(a)(1), 102(a)(2)) and related exceptions, and for formulating, defending, or overcoming rejections based on those provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation / 'described' requirement under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102
rubrics_metrics.description: The two basic requirements that must be met by a prior art document in order to describe a claimed invention such that it is anticipated under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 are: (1) 'each and every element of the claimed invention' must be disclosed either explicitly or inherently, and the elements must be 'arranged or combined in the same way as in the claim;' and (2) a person of ordinary skill in the art must have been enabled to make the invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Gleave; Eli Lilly; NetMoneyIN; In re Bond; enablement for anticipation judged from the viewpoint of a person of ordinary skill (In re Donohue). There is no requirement that a prior art document meet the 'how to use' requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) to anticipate (cases: Schoenwald; Schering; Impax Labs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation may be shown by a single species/embodiment
rubrics_metrics.description: For a prior art document to describe a claimed invention under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or (a)(2), the prior art need only describe and enable one skilled in the art to make a single species or embodiment of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes the broader 35 U.S.C. 112(a) written description requirement (which must support the entire claimed scope) from anticipation (Vas-Cath; In re Lukach; In re Van Langenhoven; In re Ruscetta). A disclosure of a single embodiment can anticipate broadly claimed subject matter for anticipation purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use as prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public use rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) may be based on uses that are public anywhere in the world; a public use must occur before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to constitute prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No geographic limitation under AIA (contrast pre-AIA §102(b) 'in this country'). Examiner should require the applicant to show that a potentially public use did not make the claimed process accessible to the public. Pre-AIA doctrines on readiness for patenting and whether use was 'accessible to the public' or 'commercially exploited' inform analysis (cases: Invitrogen; American Seating; Woodland Trust). Certain uses by the inventor or joint inventor within one year may fall under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) exceptions (see MPEP §2154.02).

rubrics_metrics.name: On sale activity as prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: On sale rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) may be based on sales or offers for sale without regard to where the sale activity took place; the phrase 'on sale' in AIA 102(a)(1) is treated as having the same meaning as 'on sale' in pre-AIA 102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-AIA Pfaff test applies: (1) subject of commercial sale or offer for sale not primarily for experimental purposes; and (2) ready for patenting. Contract/commercial law principles apply (Medicines Co. v. Hospira). Secret commercial activity can still qualify as 'on sale' (Helsinn decision: sale to third party obligated to keep confidential may qualify). Exceptions in 102(b)(1) may apply for inventor-originated sales within one year.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Otherwise available to the public' (catch-all) under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention is not entitled to a patent if it was 'otherwise available to the public' before its effective filing date — this focuses on whether the disclosure was 'available to the public' rather than the means by which it became available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include student theses in libraries, poster displays at scientific meetings, laid-open patent applications/patents, documents electronically posted on the Internet, and commercial transactions that are not sales. Even if not a printed publication or sale, the disclosure may be prior art under this provision provided the claimed invention was made sufficiently available to the public (cases: Cronyn; Hall; Bayer; Klopfenstein; Voter Verified; In re Lister; SRI Int'l; Group One).

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement that prior art be 'by others' under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A key difference from pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) is that under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) there is no requirement that the prior art relied upon be 'by others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any prior art falling under 102(a)(1) need not be by another to constitute prior art. However, disclosures made one year or less before the effective filing date by the inventor, a joint inventor, or another who obtained the subject matter from the inventor may fall within exceptions in 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions by the applicant as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Admissions by the applicant (statements in the specification or made during prosecution identifying the work of another as 'prior art') will be treated as prior art under the AIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such admissions can be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations regardless of whether the admitted prior art would otherwise qualify under 35 U.S.C. 102 (cases: Riverwood; Constant). See MPEP §2129 for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'disclosure' in AIA context
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office treats the term 'disclosure' as a generic expression intended to encompass the documents and activities enumerated in AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) (being patented, described in a printed publication, in public use, on sale, otherwise available to the public, or described in a U.S. patent, U.S. patent application publication, or WIPO published application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AIA does not define 'disclosure' explicitly; 102(b)(1) and (b)(2) condition under which a 'disclosure' that otherwise falls within 102(a)(1) or (a)(2) is not prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for determining whether to apply 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner should first consider whether the reference qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) and then whether any exceptions in 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) apply; separately, the examiner should consider whether the reference qualifies under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) and whether any exceptions in 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2) apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under 102(a)(1): patents, printed publications, public use, on sale, and otherwise making available qualify if reference predates effective filing date (sale/use need not occur in U.S.). Disclosures within one-year grace period may be excepted by 102(b)(1)(A) or (B) if made by inventor/joint inventor or derived from them. Under 102(a)(2): U.S. patents, U.S. patent application publications, and certain PCT publications are prior art if the disclosure's effectively filed date is before the claimed invention's effective filing date; see 35 U.S.C. 102(d) and MPEP §2154 for 'effectively filed' criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) (one-year grace period exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures in potential prior art references within the one-year grace period are excepted under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1)(A) if the disclosure was the inventor’s or at least one joint inventor’s own work publicly disclosed by the inventor/joint inventor or another who obtained the subject matter from them; and under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1)(B) if the reference discloses subject matter previously publicly disclosed by the inventor/joint inventor or a derivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both require that the disclosure was made one year or less before the effective filing date and involve attribution/derivation from the inventor or joint inventor. See MPEP §§2153.01(a) and 2153.02 and MPEP §717.01(b)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2) (for 102(a)(2) references)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures are not prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) if one of the three exceptions of 102(b)(2) applies: (A) limits use of an inventor’s own work disclosed in a U.S. patent/application published by another who derived the subject matter from the inventor; (B) excepts subject matter effectively filed by another after the subject matter had been publicly disclosed by the inventor/joint inventor/derivative; (C) excepts disclosures if, not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention, the disclosed subject matter and the claimed invention 'were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 102(b)(2)(C) concerns common ownership and resembles but differs from pre-AIA 103(c). See MPEP §2154.02(b) and §717.02 for joint research agreement/common ownership guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 102(a)(2) 'effectively filed' requirement and related criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. patents, U.S. patent application publications, and certain WIPO publications are prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) if the effectively filed date of the disclosure is before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if issue/publication date is not before the claimed effective filing date (so it would not qualify as 102(a)(1)), the reference may still be applicable as 102(a)(2) if it was 'effectively filed' earlier. See 35 U.S.C. 102(d) and MPEP §2154 for criteria to determine when subject matter was effectively filed and when common ownership or derivation exceptions apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to arguing patentable distinction or amending claims, a 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2) rejection can be overcome by: (A) submitting a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 120 within time and establishing the prior application satisfies 35 U.S.C. 112(a); (B) submitting a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) (provisional) within time and establishing 112(a) support; (C) submitting a priority claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) with required documentation and establishing the foreign priority application satisfies 112(a); (D) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.130 to show an applied disclosure is excepted under 35 U.S.C. 102(b); or (E) establishing common ownership or a Joint Research Agreement to obtain the 102(b)(2)(C) exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each route has procedural requirements (corrected application data sheet under 37 CFR 1.76; time limits under 37 CFR 1.78/1.55; proof of enablement/written description under 35 U.S.C. 112(a); petitions for delayed benefit/priority where applicable). See MPEP §§211, 213-216, 717, 2155, 2154.02(c). Note these methods can also overcome 103 rejections based on 102(a)(1)/(a)(2) prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prescribed form paragraphs for rejections under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102
rubrics_metrics.description: Office form paragraphs (e.g., ¶7.06; ¶7.07.aia; ¶7.08.aia; ¶7.12.aia; ¶7.14.aia; ¶7.15.01.aia) should be used when making appropriate rejections and certain instructions apply regarding their use and sequencing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of guidance: ¶7.06 must be used in all Office Actions when a prior art rejection is made in an application with actual filing date on/after March 16, 2013, that claims priority to an application filed before March 16, 2013 (use only once). ¶7.07.aia quotes 35 U.S.C. 102 and is required in first actions on the merits and final rejections; ¶7.08.aia for 102(a)(1) activity must be preceded by 7.03.aia and 7.07.aia; ¶7.12.aia for 102(a)(2) references must be preceded by 7.03.aia and 7.07.aia (and may also require 7.08.aia); ¶7.14.aia addresses pre-AIA 102(g) priority language and must be used with appropriate preceding paragraphs. Form paragraph instructions also include bracket insertions for claim numbers and prior art identification.
